analysis.one_liner: Bans oil and gas leasing in the Arctic Ocean off Alaska's coast.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban Arctic Ocean drilling never got a vote; it sat in the House Natural Resources Committee from June 2023 until Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write a permanent ban into law on issuing or renewing any federal lease or permit for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in the Arctic Ocean, including the Beaufort and Chukchi Seas off Alaska. It amends the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, so future administrations could not simply reverse the policy. It never received a hearing or a vote in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities along Alaska's Arctic coast and everyone who depends on a healthy ocean and a stable climate would gain, because the bill would keep offshore drilling out of the Arctic Ocean permanently. Native villages and fishing economies would avoid the risk of oil spills in icy, remote waters where cleanup is nearly impossible, and consumers of coastal fisheries and tourism would be protected from a spill's ripple effects.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Alaska coastal communities and coastal economies

how_it_helps.text: The bill would bar the Interior Department from issuing or renewing any lease or authorization for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in the Arctic Ocean, including the Beaufort Sea and Chukchi Sea Planning Areas.

Because the ban would be written into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act itself, it could not be undone by a future administration with a new leasing plan, giving coastal communities a durable shield rather than a policy that changes every four years.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to potential leases in the Arctic Ocean, and the federal government would forgo any future royalty revenue from that area. Regions dependent on oil-sector jobs and revenue could see less future activity, though there was no active development blocked at the time beyond areas already under leasing decisions.

drawbacks.text: Blocking Arctic leases would forgo future domestic oil and gas production and the federal royalties and jobs that come with it, an honest cost for an energy-producing region and for anyone concerned about supply and prices.
The bill is a flat prohibition with no phase-out or compensation mechanism, so it eliminates rather than manages the tradeoff between Arctic development and spill risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is permanent protection of a fragile, spill-prone ocean environment at the cost of potential oil and gas development in a remote area that has seen little production. Given that Arctic oil spills are widely understood to be nearly impossible to clean up in ice and darkness, and that the oil industry already holds vast undeveloped leases elsewhere, the tradeoff favors protection for ordinary people and coastal economies.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Natural Resources Committee, which never held a hearing or a vote on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Huffman introduced the Stop Arctic Ocean Drilling Act on June 12, 2023, with 11 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
It attracted 15 cosponsors in total, all Democrats, and no further action was ever taken; the committee never scheduled it, and it never reached the House floor.
When the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies that want access to Arctic Ocean leases are better off, since nothing now prevents a future administration from offering them. Communities that wanted a permanent drilling ban gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies wanting Arctic access

for.name: Rep. Jared Huffman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban Arctic Ocean oil and gas leasing.

for.name: 15 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, including original cosponsors Levin, Kim of New Jersey, Bonamici, Barragan, Khanna, Connolly, Beyer, Peters, Brownley, Blumenauer, and Jayapal.

against.name: Chair Bruce Westerman
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in the Natural Resources Committee he chaired for the rest of the Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote, which kept it off the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported the bill; with Republicans controlling the House and its committees, it never moved.

industries.note: The bill would take Arctic Ocean leasing permanently off the table, ending any chance of future exploration or production in the Beaufort and Chukchi Seas. Its interests run against coastal communities that bear the spill risk, since drilling profits are private while spill costs and climate damage fall on the public.

industries.industry: Commercial fishing and Alaska coastal economies
industries.note: A permanent drilling ban would protect fisheries and coastal livelihoods from the risk of an Arctic oil spill, which icy, remote conditions would make nearly impossible to clean up.
